topics.title: Athens and the first democracy
topics.intro: In about 508 BC the Athenians began an experiment: government by the citizens themselves. It was the world’s first democracy, but “the people” meant far fewer people than you might think.
topics.teach: Explain how Athenian democracy was different from democracy in Britain today.
topics.talk: Ask {her} who could NOT vote in Athens, and whether that makes it a real democracy.

topics.title: Sparta: a city built for war
topics.intro: Sparta was Athens’ great rival: ruled by two kings, its boys trained for war from the age of seven, and its economy rested on the forced labour of the helots.
topics.teach: Explain why Sparta needed such a powerful army.
topics.talk: Ask {her} whether {she} would rather have grown up in Athens or Sparta, and why.

topics.title: The Persian Wars
topics.intro: Twice the vast Persian Empire invaded Greece, and twice the quarrelsome Greek cities beat it: at Marathon in 490 BC, and at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC.
topics.teach: Explain why the Greeks won at Salamis even though the Persian fleet was larger.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what Herodotus is famous for, and why historians call him the “father of history”.

topics.title: Alexander the Great
topics.intro: Alexander of Macedon became king at 20 and in thirteen years built an empire from Greece to India. His conquests spread Greek language and ideas across the known world.
topics.teach: Explain one reason why Alexander’s empire broke up so quickly after his death.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what Alexander had in common with the heroes of Greek myth.

topics.title: Norman control and the medieval Church
topics.intro: After 1066 a few thousand Normans ruled about two million English people. Castles, the feudal system, the Domesday Book and the Church all helped them keep control.
topics.teach: Explain how the feudal system helped William keep control.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why the murder of Thomas Becket shocked medieval Europe.

topics.title: King John, Magna Carta and Parliament
topics.intro: In 1215 rebel barons forced King John to agree to Magna Carta, the first time a king of England accepted that he was under the law. Fifty years later, the first parliaments met.
topics.teach: Explain why Magna Carta still matters today.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what clause 39 of Magna Carta promised.

topics.title: The Black Death and the Peasants’ Revolt
topics.intro: In 1348 the plague reached England and killed perhaps a third to a half of the people. The survivors found their labour was suddenly precious, and in 1381 the peasants rose up.
topics.teach: Explain how the Black Death helped cause the Peasants’ Revolt.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what medieval people thought caused the plague, and what really did.

topics.title: The Tudors and the Reformation
topics.intro: In sixteenth-century Europe the Church split into Catholic and Protestant. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome, and his three children took the country in three different religious directions.
topics.teach: Explain why Henry VIII broke with the Catholic Church.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what the “middle way” of Elizabeth I was.

topics.title: Stuarts, Civil War and the Glorious Revolution
topics.intro: A king who believed God had chosen him clashed with a Parliament that controlled the money. The result was civil war, a king’s execution, eleven years without a monarch, and in 1688 a revolution that put Parliament in charge.
topics.teach: Explain the main causes of the English Civil War.
topics.talk: Ask {her} whether Oliver Cromwell was a hero or a villain.

topics.title: The Enlightenment and the French Revolution
topics.intro: Enlightenment thinkers argued that reason, not tradition, should decide how people are governed. In 1789 France put the idea into practice, with dramatic and violent results.
topics.teach: Explain how Enlightenment ideas helped cause the French Revolution.

topics.title: The Industrial Revolution
topics.intro: From about 1750, Britain became the first country to industrialise: steam power, factories, canals and railways transformed how people lived and worked, for better and for worse.
topics.talk: Ask {her} what life was like for a child working in a cotton mill around 1800.

topics.title: Empire, the slave trade and abolition
topics.intro: Britain built the largest empire in history. For more than two centuries part of its wealth came from the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans, until enslaved people’s resistance and a long campaign brought it to an end.
topics.teach: Explain the different groups who helped bring about abolition, including enslaved people themselves.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why the British government paid compensation to slave owners but not to the people who had been enslaved.

topics.title: Reform and the fight for the vote
topics.intro: In 1830 only about one adult in ten could vote. A century of campaigning, from the Chartists to the suffragists and suffragettes, changed that.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the suffragists and the suffragettes.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which was more effective: peaceful persuasion or direct action?

topics.title: The First World War
topics.intro: The war that began in 1914 was fought on an industrial scale. Millions served in the trenches, women took on new work at home, and the world that came out of it in 1918 was very different.
topics.teach: Explain the long-term causes of the First World War (militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism).
topics.talk: On Remembrance Sunday, talk with {her} about why we still remember the war.

topics.title: The Second World War and the Holocaust
topics.intro: From 1939 to 1945 the world was at war again. In the shadow of the war, Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews and persecuted many others: the Holocaust. We study it to remember the victims and to understand how it could happen.
topics.teach: Explain how Nazi persecution of Jewish people grew step by step from 1933.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why Holocaust Memorial Day is held on 27 January.

topics.title: Thinking like a historian
topics.intro: Historians don’t just know facts. They explain causes and consequences, judge change and significance, and question their sources: who made this, when, and why?
topics.teach: Explain what “provenance” means and why it matters.
topics.talk: Show {her} a newspaper headline and ask what its purpose is, and whether that makes it unreliable.

topics.title: Sources and interpretations, GCSE style
topics.intro: At GCSE you will judge how useful a source is from its content AND its provenance, and explain why historians’ interpretations differ. Here is a head start.
topics.teach: Explain how a biased source can still be useful.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why two historians might disagree about the same event.

topics.title: The Cold War
topics.intro: After 1945 the USA and the USSR, allies against Hitler, became rivals. For forty-five years they competed in arms, space and ideas, and came close to nuclear war, without fighting each other directly.
topics.teach: Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War.
topics.talk: Ask {her} why it was called a “cold” war.

topics.title: Baghdad and the Islamic Golden Age
topics.intro: While much of Europe was in the early Middle Ages, Baghdad was one of the greatest cities in the world, where scholars translated Greek books and made new discoveries in maths, medicine and science.
topics.teach: Explain how Greek learning reached medieval Europe through the Islamic world.
topics.talk: Ask {her} which English words come from Arabic (algebra, algorithm, alchemy…).

items.prompt: In about which year did Cleisthenes’ reforms create democracy in Athens?
items.explain: Cleisthenes reorganised the citizens in about 508–507 BC, giving power to the assembly.

items.prompt: The word “democracy” comes from two Greek words. What do they mean?
items.explain: dēmos = the people, kratos = power or rule.

items.prompt: Who could vote in the Athenian assembly?

options.text: Adult male citizens only
Every adult living in Athens
options.feedback: Women, slaves and foreign residents (metics) were all excluded.

options.text: Only rich landowners
options.feedback: Poor citizens could vote too: that was the radical part.

items.explain: Perhaps only 10–20% of the people of Athens were adult male citizens.

items.prompt: How was Athenian democracy different from British democracy today?

options.text: Citizens voted on laws themselves instead of electing MPs
A prime minister led the assembly and chose all of its laws
options.feedback: There was no prime minister; the assembly of citizens decided.

options.text: Athenians elected a parliament every five years
options.feedback: They met in person on the Pnyx hill and voted on laws themselves.

items.explain: Britain is a representative democracy: we elect MPs to decide for us. Athens was direct.

items.prompt: Each year Athenians could vote to exile a too-powerful citizen for ten years by scratching his name on a piece of pottery. What was this called?
items.explain: The pottery shards were called ostraka, which gives us the English word “ostracise”.

items.prompt: How were most Athenian officials and jurors chosen?

options.text: By lot (random selection)
By election, held every single year
options.feedback: Generals were elected, but most posts were filled by lot, which Athenians thought fairer.

options.text: By the richest families, in turn
options.feedback: Athens had no such system; choosing by lot was meant to stop the rich taking every post.

items.explain: Choosing by lot stopped the rich and famous from taking every job.

items.prompt: Which Athenian leader of the 440s–430s BC is linked with the building of the Parthenon?
items.explain: Pericles led Athens at the height of its power; the Parthenon was built 447–432 BC.

items.prompt: The Parthenon on the Acropolis was a temple to which goddess?
items.explain: Athena was the patron goddess of Athens, the city named after her.

items.prompt: What was the agora?

options.text: The city’s open market and meeting place
A three-banked Athenian warship with a ram
options.feedback: That was a trireme.

options.text: The harsh training system for Spartan boys
options.feedback: That was the agoge.

items.explain: The agora was where Athenians shopped, gossiped and argued about politics.

items.prompt: Was Athens a true democracy? Which answer would a top historian give?

options.text: It was revolutionary for its time, because poor citizens had real power, but it excluded most of the population, so it was a limited democracy
options.feedback: A balanced judgement that weighs both sides.

options.text: Yes, because everyone could vote
options.feedback: Not everyone: women, slaves and metics could not.

options.text: No, because women could not vote
options.feedback: True, but this ignores how radical it was to give power to poor men.

items.explain: Good historical judgements weigh evidence on both sides and reach a balanced conclusion.

items.prompt: What was the name of the tough military training Spartan boys began at about seven?
items.explain: Boys lived in barracks, were kept hungry and learned to endure pain.

items.prompt: Who were the helots?
items.answer: an enslaved people who farmed Sparta’s land
distractors: the two royal families who ruled Sparta
foreign traders who lived in Athens
Persian soldiers who settled in Greece
items.explain: The helots outnumbered Spartan citizens many times over, which is one reason Sparta needed a powerful army.

items.prompt: How was Sparta governed?

options.text: By two kings, a council of elders and elected ephors
By a direct democracy of all the citizens, just like Athens
options.feedback: Sparta was an oligarchy: rule by the few.

options.text: By a single king advised by a council of priests
options.feedback: Sparta unusually had TWO kings at once.

items.explain: Sparta mixed kingship, an elite council and elected officials: rule by the few.

items.prompt: How were Spartan women different from Athenian women?

options.text: They could own land, and girls trained in athletics
They voted in the assembly and served as magistrates
options.feedback: Neither city let women vote.

options.text: They served in the army alongside the men
options.feedback: Spartan women did not fight, but they did train their bodies.

items.explain: Sparta valued strong mothers for strong soldiers, so girls exercised and women ran estates.

items.prompt: Why did Sparta need such a powerful army?

options.text: To control the far larger helot population
Because the Spartans had no farms of their own
options.feedback: They had farms, worked by the helots.

options.text: Because Athens forced them to defend Greece
options.feedback: Sparta chose its own path.

items.explain: Fear of a helot revolt shaped the whole of Spartan society.

items.prompt: Which long war between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BC) ended in Sparta’s victory?
items.explain: The historian Thucydides wrote its history; Athens finally surrendered in 404 BC.

items.prompt: What was a phalanx?

options.text: A tight block of soldiers with overlapping shields
A Spartan festival honouring soldiers killed in war
options.feedback: It was a battle formation.

options.text: A fast warship with three banks of oars
options.feedback: That was a trireme; a phalanx was a battle formation.

items.explain: Each soldier’s shield partly protected the man to his left, so the line depended on everyone holding firm.

items.prompt: In which year did the Athenians defeat the Persians at the Battle of Marathon?
items.explain: Darius I’s invasion was beaten by an Athenian army, with help from Plataea.

items.prompt: Which Persian king sent the army defeated at Marathon?
items.explain: Darius’s son Xerxes led the second, much larger invasion in 480 BC.

items.prompt: Which Spartan king led the stand at the pass of Thermopylae in 480 BC?
items.explain: Leonidas and his 300 Spartans, with several thousand other Greeks at first, held the pass for three days.

items.prompt: How did the Persians finally get past the Greeks at Thermopylae?

options.text: A local man showed them a mountain path behind the Greeks
options.feedback: His name was Ephialtes.

options.text: Their larger fleet landed troops behind the Greek line
options.feedback: Thermopylae was a land battle in a narrow pass.

options.text: The Spartans finally ran out of food and water after three days
options.feedback: They were outflanked by a hidden path.

items.explain: The pass was narrow enough for a few to hold, until they were surrounded.

items.prompt: Which sea battle in 480 BC, planned by Themistocles, destroyed much of the Persian fleet?
items.explain: The Greeks lured the Persian ships into narrow straits where their numbers did not help.

items.prompt: Why did the Greeks win at Salamis even though the Persians had more ships?

options.text: In the narrow straits the Persian ships got in each other’s way
options.feedback: And the Greek triremes rammed them.

options.text: The Persian ships had no trained sailors on board
options.feedback: They had excellent Phoenician sailors.

options.text: A great storm had sunk most of the Persian fleet first
options.feedback: Storms had hurt the Persians earlier, but Salamis was won by tactics.

items.explain: Themistocles chose the battlefield so that numbers did not matter.

items.prompt: What was a Greek warship with three rows of oars, and a bronze ram on the front, called?
items.explain: About 170 rowers powered each trireme.

items.prompt: Which writer, called “the father of history”, wrote an account of the Persian Wars?
items.explain: Herodotus travelled widely and asked questions: his word “historiai” means “enquiries”.

items.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
items.explain: In BC dates, bigger numbers are earlier. Plataea in 479 BC ended the invasion.

items.prompt: What does the story of Pheidippides tell historians about Marathon?

options.text: It shows how the battle was later remembered, not what happened
options.feedback: It is a later legend.

options.text: It proves that a runner carried news of victory 26 miles to Athens
options.feedback: The 26-mile run to Athens appears only in much later writers.

options.text: Nothing at all, because legends are useless to historians
options.feedback: Legends are useful evidence of how people remembered events.

items.explain: Herodotus says Pheidippides ran to Sparta for help; the run back to Athens with news of victory comes from writers centuries later.

items.prompt: Which kingdom, north of Greece, was Alexander the Great from?
items.explain: Alexander was born in 356 BC, son of Philip II of Macedon.

items.prompt: Which famous philosopher was Alexander’s teacher?
items.explain: Aristotle taught the young prince for about three years.

items.prompt: Which great city in Egypt did Alexander found in 331 BC?
items.explain: Alexandria became famous for its lighthouse and its great library.

items.prompt: What was the name of Alexander’s famous horse?
items.explain: Legend says only the young Alexander could tame him, because he noticed the horse was afraid of its own shadow.

items.prompt: How old was Alexander when he died in Babylon in 323 BC?
items.explain: In just thirteen years as king he had conquered an empire stretching to India.

items.prompt: Which empire did Alexander conquer, defeating King Darius III?

options.text: The Persian Empire
The Roman Empire
options.feedback: Rome was not yet a great power.

options.text: The Chinese Empire
options.feedback: Alexander never reached China.

items.explain: Victories at Issus (333 BC) and Gaugamela (331 BC) brought down Persia.

items.prompt: What was Alexander’s most lasting legacy?

options.text: Greek language and culture spread across the East
options.feedback: This was the Hellenistic world.

options.text: A single empire that his heirs held for 500 years
options.feedback: His empire split between his generals soon after he died.

options.text: He spread Athenian democracy to every city he took
options.feedback: Democracy was Athenian, 170 years earlier, and Alexander ruled as a king.

items.explain: For centuries afterwards, Greek was the shared language of the eastern Mediterranean: even the New Testament was written in it.

items.prompt: Why did Alexander’s empire break up so quickly?

options.text: He died young with no adult heir, and his generals fought
The Romans conquered it within a year of his death
options.feedback: Rome took over parts only much later.

options.text: He divided it between his sons in his will
options.feedback: His generals (the Successors) divided it by war.

items.explain: Empires built around one brilliant individual often struggle when that person dies.

items.prompt: How did the feudal system help William control England?

options.text: He gave land to barons in return for loyalty and knights
options.feedback: And they did the same down the chain.

options.text: Every landowner voted to accept William as king
options.feedback: He won the crown by conquest.

options.text: Peasants bought their own land and paid him rent directly
options.feedback: Most peasants were villeins, tied to their lord’s land.

items.explain: Land was exchanged for loyalty and service: king, barons, knights, peasants.

items.prompt: Which great survey of land and property did William order, completed in 1086?
items.explain: It recorded who held what, so William knew how much tax he could raise.

items.prompt: What was the Harrying of the North (1069–70)?

options.text: William’s burning of the north to crush rebellion
A Scottish invasion that William drove back
options.feedback: It was William’s own campaign.

options.text: A peaceful survey of northern land and its value for taxes
options.feedback: It was brutal: many people starved.

items.explain: Chroniclers recorded famine and death across Yorkshire. It was harsh, and effective.

items.prompt: Why did the Normans build motte and bailey castles so quickly after 1066?

options.text: Earth and timber made them quick to build
options.feedback: From them a few soldiers could control the area.

options.text: They were made of stone, which was quick to cut
options.feedback: Stone keeps came later; the first castles were timber.

options.text: They were built as homes for English nobles
options.feedback: They were bases to dominate the English.

items.explain: Around 500 castles were built in William’s reign.

items.prompt: What was the tithe that peasants paid to the Church?
distractors: one half of all their land
items.explain: The Church was enormously rich and powerful in medieval England.

items.prompt: Which Archbishop of Canterbury was murdered in his cathedral in 1170 after quarrelling with Henry II?
items.explain: Four knights killed him after hearing the king’s angry words. Becket became a saint, and Canterbury a great pilgrimage site.

items.prompt: Why did Henry II and Becket quarrel?

options.text: Over whether clergy accused of crimes faced the king’s courts
Over who should marry the king’s eldest daughter
options.feedback: It was about power: Church versus Crown.

options.text: Over whether Henry should lead a crusade
options.feedback: The quarrel was about law and power in England.

items.explain: The dispute was about who had more power in England: the king or the Church.

items.prompt: What was the purpose of a medieval “doom painting” on a church wall?

options.text: To show people who could not read what heaven and hell were like
To decorate a lord’s castle hall with scenes of battle
options.feedback: Doom paintings were in churches.

options.text: To record who owned what land in the Domesday survey
options.feedback: Different “doom”: it means judgement.

items.explain: Pictures taught a mostly illiterate population about the Last Judgement.

items.prompt: In which year did King John agree to Magna Carta?
items.explain: At Runnymede, by the River Thames, in June 1215.

items.prompt: In which meadow beside the Thames was Magna Carta agreed?
items.explain: Runnymede is near Windsor.

items.prompt: Why were the barons so angry with King John?

options.text: He lost his French lands, then taxed heavily to win them back
options.feedback: He also quarrelled with the Pope.

options.text: He refused to join his brother Richard on crusade
options.feedback: That was not the main grievance.

options.text: He gave peasants the right to vote for Parliament
options.feedback: Nobody had a vote then.

items.explain: Losing Normandy in 1204, then taxing heavily to win it back, turned the barons against him.

items.prompt: What did clause 39 of Magna Carta promise?

options.text: No free man would be jailed except by lawful judgement
options.feedback: By the lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land.

options.text: Every free man could vote for the king’s council
options.feedback: Voting came centuries later.

options.text: No taxes could ever again be raised by the king
options.feedback: Taxes needed consent, not abolition.

items.explain: This idea, that the king is under the law, still underpins British and American law.

items.prompt: Why is Magna Carta still seen as significant?

options.text: It set the principle that even the king is under the law
It gave every single person in England equal rights in 1215
options.feedback: It mostly protected barons and free men, not villeins.

options.text: It ended royal power and handed rule to the barons
options.feedback: England kept its kings.

items.explain: Its importance grew over time as later generations reinterpreted it.

items.prompt: In 1265 which rebel baron called a parliament that included representatives of the towns for the first time?
items.explain: De Montfort’s parliament is often seen as a step towards the House of Commons.

items.prompt: In which year did the Black Death reach England?
items.explain: It arrived at Melcombe (now Weymouth) in Dorset in the summer of 1348.

items.prompt: About what proportion of England’s people died in the Black Death?

options.text: Perhaps a third to a half
About one in a hundred
options.feedback: It was far worse than that.

options.text: Everyone except the king
options.feedback: Many survived, but losses were enormous.

items.explain: Historians’ estimates vary, but somewhere between 30% and 50% is usual.

items.prompt: What do we now know caused the Black Death?

options.text: Bacteria (Yersinia pestis) carried by rat fleas
options.feedback: It also spread between people.

options.text: Bad air (miasma) rising from rotting rubbish
options.feedback: That was the medieval “miasma” theory.

options.text: An unlucky alignment of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars
options.feedback: Some medieval doctors believed this, but it is wrong.

items.explain: Medieval people blamed God’s punishment, bad air or the stars. Germ theory came 500 years later.

items.prompt: Why did some people called flagellants whip themselves in public?

options.text: They hoped to win God’s forgiveness and end the plague
They wanted to spread the disease to their enemies
options.feedback: They thought they were stopping it.

options.text: Courts had sentenced them to it as a punishment for theft
options.feedback: It was voluntary religious penance.

items.explain: Religion shaped how medieval people understood disaster.

items.prompt: How did the Black Death change life for surviving peasants?

options.text: Scarce labour let peasants demand higher wages
Many were made knights to replace the dead lords
options.feedback: They stayed peasants, but with more bargaining power.

options.text: Wages fell because there was less work to do
options.feedback: The opposite: labour shortages pushed wages up and shook the feudal system.

items.explain: The government tried to freeze wages with the Statute of Labourers (1351), which caused resentment.

items.prompt: In which year did the Peasants’ Revolt take place?
items.explain: Rebels from Essex and Kent marched on London in June 1381.

items.prompt: What was the short-term trigger of the Peasants’ Revolt?

options.text: A third poll tax, charged on everyone over 15
A new law forcing peasants to fight in France
options.feedback: There was no such law; the poll tax was the spark.

options.text: The king’s order to close all village markets
options.feedback: There was no such order; the poll tax was the spark.

items.explain: Long-term causes included anger over wages and serfdom; the poll tax was the spark.

items.prompt: Which leader of the Peasants’ Revolt was killed while meeting the king at Smithfield?
items.explain: He was struck down by the Lord Mayor of London, William Walworth.

items.prompt: How old was King Richard II when he faced the rebels in 1381?
items.explain: The boy king promised the rebels freedom, then broke his promises once they went home.

items.prompt: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” What was the preacher John Ball arguing?

options.text: That God made all equal, so no one should be a serf
That men should farm while women spin the wool
options.feedback: It is a question about equality.

options.text: That Adam and Eve had been the very first English peasants
options.feedback: It is about equality, not English history.

items.explain: At the start of the world, Adam dug and Eve spun: nobody was a lord. So why should anyone be a serf?

items.prompt: Which German monk began the Reformation in 1517 by criticising the Church?
items.explain: His 95 Theses attacked the sale of indulgences (pardons for sin).

items.prompt: Why did Henry VIII break with the Catholic Church?

options.text: The Pope would not annul his marriage, and he wanted a son
options.feedback: He also wanted control of the Church and its wealth.

options.text: Henry had become a convinced Lutheran Protestant
options.feedback: Henry had attacked Luther and stayed Catholic in many beliefs.

options.text: The Pope had sent an army to invade England
options.feedback: There was no invasion.

items.explain: The break was about Henry’s marriage, his need for a son, power and money, more than belief.

items.prompt: Which 1534 Act made Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England?
items.explain: Refusing to accept Henry’s new position was treason: Sir Thomas More was executed in 1535.

items.prompt: Why did Henry VIII close the monasteries between 1536 and 1541?

options.text: To take their wealth and end loyalty to the Pope
Because most monks asked to leave and marry
options.feedback: Most did not.

options.text: To turn every monastery into a free grammar school
options.feedback: A few schools were founded, but money and power were the main motives.

items.explain: Thomas Cromwell organised the Dissolution. The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) rose partly in protest.

items.prompt: Put these Tudor monarchs in order of their reigns.
items.explain: Henry’s three children ruled in turn: Edward, Mary, then Elizabeth.

items.prompt: What did Mary I try to do?

options.text: Return England to the Catholic Church
Make England strictly Protestant
options.feedback: That was her brother Edward VI.

options.text: Abolish religion
options.feedback: No Tudor tried that.

items.explain: Around 280 Protestants were burned for heresy in her reign, earning her the name “Bloody Mary” from Protestant writers.

items.prompt: What was Elizabeth I’s “middle way” (the religious settlement of 1559)?

options.text: A Protestant Church that kept some Catholic traditions
Complete freedom to follow whichever religion you chose
options.feedback: Everyone still had to attend the Church of England.

options.text: A Catholic Church that obeyed the Pope again
options.feedback: It was Protestant, but moderate.

items.explain: She wanted outward loyalty and peace rather than perfect agreement in belief.

items.prompt: What important change happened in English churches in 1539?
items.answer: an English Bible was placed in every parish church
distractors: every parish church was closed for a year
all services were held in French, not Latin
the Pope visited England to bless the king
items.explain: The Great Bible meant ordinary people could hear and read the Bible in their own language.

items.prompt: In which year did Catholic plotters try to blow up King James I and Parliament?
items.explain: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding the gunpowder on 5 November 1605.

items.prompt: What did Charles I believe about his power?

options.text: God had chosen him, so he answered only to God
options.feedback: This is the Divine Right of Kings.

options.text: Parliament should share power and approve all taxes
options.feedback: That was what his opponents wanted.

options.text: The people should elect each new king
options.feedback: Not in the 1600s!

items.explain: Charles ruled without Parliament for eleven years (1629–40).

items.prompt: Which was NOT a cause of the English Civil War?

options.text: A French invasion of England
Arguments over money and taxes such as Ship Money
options.feedback: This WAS a cause.

options.text: Fears that Charles was making the Church too Catholic
options.feedback: This WAS a cause.

options.text: Charles’s belief in the Divine Right of Kings
options.feedback: This WAS a cause.

items.explain: Money, religion and power together caused the war.

items.prompt: In which year did the English Civil War begin?
items.explain: Charles raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642.

items.prompt: Who were the “Roundheads” and the “Cavaliers”?

options.text: Supporters of Parliament and supporters of the king
The English army and the invading Scottish army
options.feedback: Both sides were mostly English.

options.text: Catholic rebels and the king’s Protestant army
options.feedback: Both sides were largely Protestant.

items.explain: The nicknames came from short haircuts (Roundheads) and fashionable riders (Cavaliers).

items.prompt: At which battle in 1645 did the New Model Army decisively defeat the king?
items.explain: After Naseby, the royalist cause collapsed.

items.prompt: In which year was Charles I executed?
items.explain: He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649.

items.prompt: Who ruled as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658?
items.explain: Not to be confused with Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII’s minister a century earlier.

items.prompt: Why do historians disagree about Oliver Cromwell?

options.text: He defended Parliament but ruled through the army and was brutal in Ireland
Almost no written records of his life or rule have survived to today
options.feedback: His life is very well recorded.

options.text: He crowned himself king, which some saw as a betrayal
options.feedback: He refused the crown in 1657.

items.explain: Interpretations differ because his actions really were mixed: a good chance to weigh evidence.

items.prompt: In 1660 the monarchy returned. Who became king?
items.explain: This is called the Restoration.

items.prompt: What happened in the “Glorious Revolution” of 1688?

options.text: James II was replaced by William and Mary, with limits on royal power
Charles I was tried by Parliament and executed in Whitehall
options.feedback: That was 1649.

options.text: Parliament was abolished and the army ruled the country
options.feedback: Parliament became stronger.

items.explain: The Bill of Rights (1689) meant monarchs could not tax or keep an army in peacetime without Parliament’s consent.

items.prompt: What was the central idea of the Enlightenment?

options.text: That reason and evidence, not tradition, should guide us
That kings were chosen by God and must be obeyed
options.feedback: Enlightenment thinkers challenged this.

options.text: That science threatened faith and so should be strictly limited
options.feedback: They championed science.

items.explain: Thinkers such as Locke, Montesquieu and Voltaire questioned old authorities.

items.prompt: Which English philosopher argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property?
items.explain: Locke’s ideas influenced both the American and French revolutions.

items.prompt: On which date was the Bastille prison in Paris stormed, now France’s national day?
items.explain: The storming of the Bastille became the symbol of the Revolution.

items.prompt: What was the motto of the French Revolution?
items.explain: Liberté, égalité, fraternité is still France’s motto.

items.prompt: Which was a cause of the French Revolution?

options.text: The state was nearly bankrupt and bread was very expensive
options.feedback: And the Third Estate paid most taxes but had little power.

options.text: France had just won a war against Britain and was very rich
options.feedback: Helping America win independence had left France deep in debt.

options.text: The king had just given every man the right to vote
options.feedback: Ordinary people had almost no power.

items.explain: Debt, hunger, unfairness and new ideas together created a revolution.

items.prompt: Which French king was executed by guillotine in January 1793?
items.explain: His queen, Marie Antoinette, was executed in October 1793.

items.prompt: What was the Reign of Terror (1793–94)?

options.text: A time when the revolutionary government executed thousands
Napoleon’s disastrous invasion of Russia in winter
options.feedback: That was 1812.

options.text: A British naval blockade that starved French ports
options.feedback: It was violence inside France.

items.explain: Led by Robespierre, who was himself guillotined in July 1794.

items.prompt: At which battle in 1815 was Napoleon finally defeated?
items.explain: The Duke of Wellington and the Prussian commander Blücher defeated him in what is now Belgium.

items.prompt: Which reason helps explain why Britain industrialised first?

options.text: Plentiful coal and iron, trade money and inventors
options.feedback: And a growing population to work and to buy.

options.text: Britain’s warm climate suited cotton growing
options.feedback: Climate was not the reason, and cotton was imported.

options.text: Britain had given up farming in order to build factories
options.feedback: An agricultural revolution actually helped feed the workers.

items.explain: Historians stress a mix of factors: resources, capital, markets, ideas and stability.

items.prompt: Which Scottish engineer greatly improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s?
items.explain: His separate condenser made engines far more efficient. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

items.prompt: Whose water-powered mill at Cromford (1771) is often called the first modern factory?
items.explain: Arkwright’s water frame spun cotton thread by machine.

items.prompt: Which railway, opened in 1830, was the first to carry passengers between two cities using only steam locomotives?
items.explain: Stephenson’s Rocket had won the Rainhill Trials to work on it in 1829.

items.prompt: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do?

options.text: Banned under-9s from textile mills; limited others’ hours
Banned all child labour in every kind of workplace
options.feedback: It was a first step, not a complete ban.

options.text: Gave every male factory worker over the age of 21 the vote
options.feedback: That came much later.

items.explain: Inspectors were appointed to enforce it, though there were few of them.

items.prompt: In 1854 Dr John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in London to what?

options.text: A water pump on Broad Street
Bad air from the Thames
options.feedback: Most people thought so, but Snow showed it was contaminated water.

options.text: Rats in the sewers
options.feedback: His evidence pointed to the water pump.

items.explain: Snow mapped the deaths and found them clustered round the pump: an early triumph of evidence.

items.prompt: Who were the Luddites (1811–16)?

options.text: Workers who smashed machines they feared would replace them
Factory owners who paid for new canals and roads
options.feedback: They were skilled workers protesting.

options.text: A company that built the first passenger railway
options.feedback: They were protesters.

items.explain: Today a “Luddite” means someone who resists new technology.

items.prompt: Was the Industrial Revolution good for ordinary people? Which is the strongest answer?

options.text: In the short term many suffered from dangerous work and crowded, unhealthy towns, but in the long run living standards rose greatly
options.feedback: A balanced judgement that considers time scale.

options.text: Yes, everyone got rich
options.feedback: Many workers lived in terrible conditions.

options.text: No, it only made things worse
options.feedback: For many at first, yes; but long-term wages, health and life expectancy improved.

items.explain: Strong answers consider different groups and different time scales.

items.prompt: What was the “triangular trade”?

options.text: Goods to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, sugar home
options.feedback: Cotton and tobacco came back to Britain too.

options.text: A treaty trade between Britain, France and Spain
options.feedback: It linked Europe, Africa and the Americas.

options.text: A trade in tea between Britain, India and China
options.feedback: It linked Europe, Africa and the Americas; it is named after the shape of the route.

items.explain: Each leg made profits for British merchants, built on the suffering of enslaved people.

items.prompt: What was the voyage of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic called?
items.explain: Enslaved people were packed in terrible conditions; many died on the voyage.

items.prompt: About how many Africans were forced onto ships across the Atlantic in the whole transatlantic slave trade?

options.text: About 12 million
About 12 thousand
options.feedback: The scale was a thousand times greater.

options.text: About 1 billion
options.feedback: That is far too many: about 12.5 million is the usual estimate.

items.explain: British ships carried around 3 million of them. Behind each number is a person.

items.prompt: Which formerly enslaved man published a best-selling autobiography in 1789 that helped the abolition campaign?
items.explain: Equiano bought his freedom, settled in Britain and campaigned against slavery.

items.prompt: Which MP led the campaign against the slave trade in Parliament?
items.explain: Wilberforce worked with campaigners such as Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp and Olaudah Equiano.

items.prompt: In which year did Britain abolish the slave TRADE?
items.explain: The trade was banned in 1807; slavery itself in the British Empire was abolished by the 1833 Act.

items.prompt: Which act abolished slavery itself in most of the British Empire?
items.explain: It came into force in 1834, but forced “apprenticeships” lasted until 1838.

items.prompt: Who received compensation when slavery was abolished in 1833?

options.text: Slave owners, who were paid £20 million
The people who had been enslaved
options.feedback: They received nothing.

options.text: No one
options.feedback: Owners were compensated; enslaved people were not.

items.explain: £20 million was about 40% of the government’s yearly budget. The loans took until 2015 to repay.

items.prompt: Which shows enslaved people’s own role in ending slavery?

options.text: The Haitian Revolution and the 1831 Jamaican rebellion
options.feedback: Samuel Sharpe led the Jamaican rebellion of 1831–32.

options.text: Parliament acting entirely on its own, with no outside pressure
options.feedback: Parliament acted, but resistance by enslaved people put real pressure on it.

options.text: Enslaved people accepting their fate until freed
options.feedback: Resistance was constant, from everyday refusal to large rebellions.

items.explain: Historians now stress that abolition was won by enslaved people as well as by British campaigners.

items.prompt: What happened after the Indian Rebellion of 1857?

options.text: The British government took direct control of India
options.feedback: Rule passed from the East India Company to the Crown: the Raj.

options.text: India became a fully independent country within a year
options.feedback: Independence came in 1947.

options.text: France took over the East India Company’s lands
options.feedback: It came under direct British rule.

items.explain: In 1876 Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India.

items.prompt: By the early 1900s, about how much of the world’s land did the British Empire cover?
items.explain: It was the largest empire in history, ruling over about 400 million people.

items.prompt: In which year did India and Pakistan become independent?
items.explain: Independence came after a long campaign led by figures such as Gandhi; partition caused terrible violence.

items.prompt: Which 1832 Act gave the vote to more middle-class men and redrew constituencies?
distractors: the Representation of the People Act of 1918
items.explain: Still only about 1 in 5 adult men could vote afterwards.

items.prompt: What did the Chartists (1838–48) campaign for?

options.text: Votes for all men and a secret ballot
Votes for all women over the age of 30
options.feedback: The People’s Charter asked for votes for all men.

options.text: An end to the monarchy and the Lords
options.feedback: Their six points were about Parliament.

items.explain: All but one of their six points (annual elections) eventually became law.

items.prompt: What was the difference between the suffragists and the suffragettes?

options.text: Suffragists campaigned peacefully; suffragettes used direct action
Suffragists wanted the vote for women; suffragettes opposed it
options.feedback: Both wanted votes for women.

options.text: They were the same group under two different names
options.feedback: Their methods were very different.

items.explain: Millicent Fawcett led the suffragists (NUWSS); Emmeline Pankhurst the suffragettes (WSPU).

items.prompt: Who led the peaceful suffragists of the NUWSS?
items.explain: Her statue stands in Parliament Square, the first statue of a woman there.

items.prompt: Who founded the Women’s Social and Political Union (the suffragettes) in 1903?
items.explain: Its motto was “Deeds not words”.

items.prompt: What happened to Emily Wilding Davison at the Epsom Derby in 1913?

options.text: She was hit by the king’s horse and died of her injuries
She rode the king’s horse to victory in the race
options.feedback: She ran onto the course during the race.

options.text: She was arrested at the course and later elected to Parliament
options.feedback: Women could not stand for Parliament until 1918.

items.explain: Historians still debate exactly what she intended.

items.prompt: In 1918 which women gained the vote?
items.answer: women over 30 meeting a property test
distractors: all women over 21, the same as men
all women over 18 who had done war work
only women who owned their own businesses
items.explain: The same Act gave the vote to all men over 21.

items.prompt: In which year did women get the vote on equal terms with men (at 21)?
items.explain: The Equal Franchise Act of 1928.

items.prompt: Why did some women get the vote in 1918?

options.text: War work changed attitudes, after decades of campaigning
The suffragettes had won a famous court case against Parliament
options.feedback: There was no such case.

options.text: Most men gave up their votes so women could vote
options.feedback: Men’s votes were extended too.

items.explain: Historians debate the weight of each factor: campaigning, war work and political change.

items.prompt: Who was the first woman to take her seat as an MP, in 1919?
items.explain: Constance Markievicz was elected first, in 1918, but as an Irish republican did not take her seat.

items.prompt: Whose assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 sparked the First World War?
items.explain: He was heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary; his killer was Gavrilo Princip.

items.prompt: What do the letters MAIN stand for, as long-term causes of the war?

options.text: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism
Money, Armies, Invasions, Navies
options.feedback: Close, but not quite.

options.text: Monarchy, Assassination, Industry, Navy
options.feedback: The assassination was the short-term trigger.

items.explain: Long-term causes made war likely; the assassination was the spark.

items.prompt: Why did Britain declare war on 4 August 1914?

options.text: Germany invaded Belgium, whose neutrality Britain guaranteed
German Zeppelins had already bombed London
options.feedback: That came later, in 1915.

options.text: Britain wanted to seize Germany’s African colonies
options.feedback: The treaty with Belgium was the official reason.

items.explain: The 1839 Treaty of London guaranteed Belgian neutrality.

items.prompt: What was the line of trenches from the Channel coast to Switzerland called?
items.explain: For most of the war it moved only a few miles either way.

items.prompt: What happened on 1 July 1916, the first day of the Battle of the Somme?

options.text: Britain suffered about 57,000 casualties in one day
options.feedback: The British Army’s worst day ever.

options.text: Germany asked for an armistice and the war soon ended
options.feedback: The battle lasted until November 1916.

options.text: British tanks broke through and won in one day
options.feedback: Tanks were first used later in the battle, in September.

items.explain: Nearly 20,000 British soldiers were killed that day. The battle became a symbol of the war’s cost.

items.prompt: Which new weapon did the British first use at the Somme in September 1916?
items.explain: Early tanks were slow and unreliable, but pointed to the future.

items.prompt: How did the war change life for women in Britain?

options.text: Many took jobs in factories, including making shells
Women were forbidden by law to take paid jobs
options.feedback: The opposite: their work was essential.

options.text: Women had to join the army and fight in the trenches of France
options.feedback: Women served as nurses and in support roles, not as fighting soldiers; over a million more went out to work.

items.explain: Women making munitions were nicknamed “munitionettes”.

items.prompt: In which year did Britain introduce conscription, forcing men to join the army?
items.explain: Until then the army relied on volunteers. Conscientious objectors refused to fight on moral grounds.

items.prompt: At what time and date did the fighting stop in 1918?
items.explain: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month: why we fall silent at 11 o’clock on Armistice Day.

items.prompt: Which soldier-poet wrote “Dulce et Decorum Est”, about a gas attack?
items.explain: Owen was killed a week before the Armistice. The title is Latin from Horace: “it is sweet and fitting (to die for your country)”.

items.prompt: What did the Treaty of Versailles (1919) make Germany do?

options.text: Accept blame, pay reparations and lose land
options.feedback: Its army was limited too.

options.text: Join the Allies in a new defensive alliance
options.feedback: Germany was treated as the defeated enemy.

options.text: Little: it was a gentle peace that Germany welcomed
options.feedback: Many Germans called it a “Diktat”: a dictated peace.

items.explain: Resentment at the treaty later helped Hitler win support: a link between the two wars.

items.prompt: Germany’s invasion of which country on 1 September 1939 led Britain to declare war?
items.explain: Britain and France declared war on 3 September 1939.

items.prompt: Who became Prime Minister in May 1940?
items.explain: Churchill replaced Chamberlain as France was being invaded.

items.prompt: Put these events of the Second World War in order.
items.explain: Dunkirk (May–June 1940), the Battle of Britain (summer 1940), Pearl Harbor (December 1941), D-Day (June 1944), VE Day (8 May 1945).

items.prompt: Why was the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 a turning point?

options.text: It brought the United States into the war
It ended the war in Europe
options.feedback: The war in Europe went on until 1945.

options.text: It was the first battle of the war
options.feedback: The war had begun in 1939.

items.explain: American industry and soldiers transformed the war.

items.prompt: At which Soviet city was a German army destroyed in the winter of 1942–43?
items.explain: Stalingrad was a turning point on the Eastern Front.

items.prompt: About how many Jewish people were murdered in the Holocaust?
items.explain: Around two thirds of Europe’s Jews. The Nazis also murdered Roma and Sinti people, disabled people and others.

items.prompt: Nazi persecution grew step by step. Put these in order.
items: Boycott of Jewish shops and businesses
items.explain: Understanding how persecution escalated in stages helps explain how the Holocaust could happen.

items.prompt: What was Kristallnacht (9–10 November 1938)?

options.text: A night of attacks on synagogues and Jewish shops
A German victory over Poland in the war’s first battle
options.feedback: It was violence against Jewish people inside Germany.

options.text: A festival of glass-making held in Berlin
options.feedback: The name means “night of broken glass”: it was a pogrom.

items.explain: Around 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps afterwards.

items.prompt: What was the name of the rescue effort that brought about 10,000 mainly Jewish children to Britain in 1938–39?
items.explain: Most of the children never saw their parents again.

items.prompt: Holocaust Memorial Day is 27 January. What happened on that day in 1945?
distractors: the war in Europe finally ended
Hitler came to power in Germany
items.explain: Auschwitz was the largest Nazi death camp; about 1.1 million people were murdered there.

items.prompt: Which Jewish girl’s diary, written while hiding in Amsterdam, is read all over the world?
items.explain: Anne was betrayed in 1944 and died in Bergen-Belsen in early 1945, aged 15.

items.prompt: On which date was VE (Victory in Europe) Day?
items.explain: The war against Japan ended in August 1945, after the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

items.prompt: Which century was the year 1066 in?
items.explain: The 11th century is the 1000s: add one to the first two digits.

items.prompt: Which is earlier: 490 BC or 323 BC?

options.text: 490 BC
323 BC
options.feedback: BC dates count down towards year 1, so the bigger number is earlier.

options.text: They are the same year
options.feedback: They are 167 years apart.

items.explain: BC years count backwards: 490 BC came 167 years before 323 BC.

items.prompt: Which is a PRIMARY source for the Battle of the Somme?

options.text: A letter written by a soldier who fought there
A history textbook about the battle, written in 2015
options.feedback: That is secondary: written later, using other sources.

options.text: A documentary about the battle made in 2006
options.feedback: That is secondary.

items.explain: Primary sources come from the time; secondary sources are later accounts and interpretations.

items.prompt: When historians ask about a source’s provenance, what do they want to know?

options.text: Who made it, when, and why
How long it is
options.feedback: Length tells you little.

options.text: Whether it has pictures
options.feedback: Provenance is about origin and purpose.

items.explain: Think NOP: Nature, Origin, Purpose.

items.prompt: A wartime poster exaggerates how happy factory workers were. Is it useless to a historian?

options.text: No: it shows what the government wanted people to think
Yes: a biased source cannot tell us anything true
options.feedback: A biased source tells you a lot about its author’s purpose.

options.text: Yes: only official written documents count as real evidence
options.feedback: Propaganda is valuable evidence.

items.explain: Utility depends on the question you ask. Bias can itself be evidence.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a long-term cause and a trigger?

options.text: Long-term causes build up; a trigger sets things off
There is no real difference: both words mean the same thing
options.feedback: Good history essays separate them.

options.text: A trigger is always the most important cause
options.feedback: Often the long-term causes matter more.

items.explain: Example: the alliance system (long-term) and Franz Ferdinand’s assassination (trigger).

items.prompt: Which question best tests whether an event was historically significant?

options.text: Did it cause big, lasting changes for many people?
Was it exciting and dramatic for people at the time?
options.feedback: Exciting events are not always significant.

options.text: Did it happen a very long time ago, before 1500?
options.feedback: Age does not make something significant.

items.explain: Historians judge significance by depth, breadth and duration of impact, and by what it reveals.

items.prompt: Which is an example of CONTINUITY between 1500 and 1800?

options.text: Most people still worked on the land
Steam engines replaced most water wheels
options.feedback: That is a change.

options.text: The Church of England was created
options.feedback: That is a change.

items.explain: Continuity means things that stayed the same while other things changed.

items.prompt: A film shows a Tudor knight checking a wristwatch. What is this mistake called?

options.text: An anachronism
An interpretation
options.feedback: An anachronism is something placed in the wrong time.

options.text: A primary source
options.feedback: It is an error of timing.

items.explain: Wristwatches became common only in the 20th century.

items.prompt: Which is a CONSEQUENCE of the Black Death, rather than a cause of it?

options.text: Peasants demanding higher wages
Fleas carried by rats
options.feedback: That helped cause the plague.

options.text: Trade ships arriving from Europe
options.feedback: That helped spread it.

items.explain: Causes come before an event; consequences come after it.

items.prompt: A 1915 British recruitment poster shows smiling soldiers. How useful is it for studying the First World War?

options.text: Useful for showing how the government tried to persuade men to join up, but not for what life at the front was really like, because its purpose was persuasion
options.feedback: This uses content AND provenance, and links usefulness to a specific enquiry.

options.text: Not useful, because it is biased
options.feedback: Biased sources are useful for studying attitudes and propaganda.

options.text: Very useful, because it shows soldiers were happy
options.feedback: It shows what the government wanted people to believe, not necessarily the truth.

items.explain: GCSE answers judge utility by both content and provenance, for a particular question.

items.prompt: Why might two historians give different interpretations of Oliver Cromwell?

options.text: They may use different sources, ask different questions, and write at different times with different concerns
options.feedback: This explains how interpretations are made.

options.text: One of them must be lying
options.feedback: Disagreement usually comes from evidence and focus, not lies.

options.text: Because history is just opinion
options.feedback: Interpretations must be supported by evidence; some are better supported than others.

items.explain: Interpretations are shaped by evidence, emphasis and context.

items.prompt: An account of the Black Death was written in 1349 by a monk. Which point about its provenance is strongest?

options.text: Written during the plague, so it shows contemporary beliefs
options.feedback: Though a monk might stress God’s punishment.

options.text: A monk wrote it, so nothing in it can be trusted
options.feedback: Monks were key record-keepers; their viewpoint needs weighing, not dismissing.

options.text: It was written long after the plague had ended
options.feedback: 1349 is during the plague.

items.explain: Weigh what the author’s position and timing add and what they might distort.

items.prompt: How can a historian check whether a source is reliable?

options.text: Compare it with other sources and known facts
Check whether it has been printed in a book
options.feedback: Printing does not make something true.

options.text: See whether its author was famous at the time
options.feedback: Fame does not make a source reliable.

items.explain: Corroboration is one of the historian’s main tools.

items.prompt: “The suffragettes were the main reason women got the vote in 1918.” Which plan would earn the highest marks?

options.text: Weigh the suffragettes against other factors (suffragists, war work, political change), then reach a supported judgement
options.feedback: This evaluates several factors and judges the relative importance.

options.text: Describe everything the suffragettes did
options.feedback: Description without judgement scores low.

options.text: Agree completely and give one example
options.feedback: One-sided answers miss the other factors.

items.explain: GCSE essays reward balance, evidence and a clear, justified conclusion.

items.prompt: What should you do FIRST when analysing a political cartoon?

options.text: Work out its date, origin and intended message
Decide whether you find it funny or not
options.feedback: Humour is a technique; the message matters.

options.text: Count and name every single person drawn in the cartoon
options.feedback: Focus on the message and context.

items.explain: Context and purpose unlock what a cartoon is saying.

items.prompt: Why was the Cold War called “cold”?

options.text: The superpowers never fought each other directly
Most of the actual fighting took place in the frozen Arctic
options.feedback: It was a global rivalry.

options.text: The battles stopped every year for the winter
options.feedback: It lasted from about 1945 to 1991.

items.explain: They fought through arms races, spying, propaganda and wars between their allies.

items.prompt: Which pair of ideologies divided the two superpowers?

options.text: Capitalism and democracy (USA) against communism (USSR)
Protestant Christianity (USA) against Orthodox Christianity (USSR)
options.feedback: It was about economic and political systems, not religion.

options.text: Monarchy (USSR) against republicanism (USA)
options.feedback: Both were republics.

items.explain: Each side believed its system was best and feared the other’s spread.

items.prompt: Who said in 1946 that an “iron curtain” had descended across Europe?
items.explain: He spoke at Fulton, Missouri.

items.prompt: What was the Berlin Airlift (1948–49)?

options.text: Western planes flew supplies into blockaded West Berlin
A huge air battle between US and Soviet jets
options.feedback: No shots were fired.

options.text: The building of the Berlin Wall to divide the city
options.feedback: That was in 1961.

items.explain: Planes landed every few minutes for almost a year.

items.prompt: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
items.explain: It was built in 1961 and opened on 9 November 1989.

items.prompt: Why was the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) so dangerous?

options.text: Soviet missiles in Cuba brought nuclear war close
Cuban troops invaded Florida and seized Miami
options.feedback: Cuba did not invade.

options.text: The Berlin Wall fell and Germany reunited
options.feedback: That was 1989.

items.explain: Kennedy and Khrushchev found a deal after thirteen tense days.

items.prompt: Which country launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957?
items.explain: Sputnik started the Space Race; the USA landed the first people on the Moon in 1969.

items.prompt: In which year did the Soviet Union break up, ending the Cold War?
items.explain: It split into 15 independent countries in December 1991.

items.prompt: Which city, founded in 762 as the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, became a world centre of learning?
items.explain: At its height it may have been the largest city in the world.

items.prompt: What was the famous library and centre of translation in Baghdad called?
items.explain: Scholars there translated Greek works by Aristotle, Euclid and Galen into Arabic.

items.prompt: Which scholar’s book gave us the word “algebra”, and whose name gave us “algorithm”?
items.explain: His book on al-jabr (restoring) laid foundations of algebra.

items.prompt: Which Persian doctor wrote “The Canon of Medicine”, used in European universities for 500 years?
items.explain: Ibn Sina built on Greek medicine and added his own observations.

items.prompt: How did many Ancient Greek books survive to reach medieval Europe?

options.text: They were translated into Arabic, then into Latin
Viking raiders carried them back north to Scandinavia
options.feedback: Arabic translations were the key route.

options.text: They lay buried under Athens until about 1900
options.feedback: Many reached Europe through Spain and Sicily in the 1100s.

items.explain: Toledo in Spain was a great centre where Arabic texts were translated into Latin.

items.prompt: Where did our “Arabic” numerals, including zero, originally come from?

options.text: India, via the Arab world
Ancient Rome, via the Byzantine Empire
options.feedback: Romans used letters: I, V, X.

options.text: Ancient Egypt, via Greek traders
options.feedback: Egyptian numerals were different symbols.

items.explain: They are sometimes called Hindu–Arabic numerals.

items.prompt: Which scholar of Cairo wrote the “Book of Optics”, showing that we see because light enters the eye?
items.explain: He tested ideas with experiments, an early step towards the scientific method.

items.prompt: Which invaders sacked Baghdad in 1258, destroying the House of Wisdom?
items.explain: Chroniclers said the River Tigris ran black with ink from the books thrown into it.
